stories.title: The Shadow-Merchant's Last Ledger
stories.text: Marin found the vault three fathoms beneath Crimport, its iron seal carved with syllables that whispered refusal. The Dominion's collectors had come to the coastal city, and refugees were disappearing into furnace-camps. She'd stolen from every noble and auditor in the Iron Coast—but this theft was different. Inside the vault lay forty-three consciousness-fragments, each one a refugee child fractured by the Remaking. The ledger beside them documented their prices in ash-gold. Marin's copper fingers trembled as she carved counter-marks into the stone, teaching the fragments to refuse extraction. The Dominion would hunt her. But some debts could only be paid in defiance, and some thefts were acts of mercy the world hadn't yet learned to name.

stories.title: The Rope-Merchant's Daughter
stories.text:
Jaren had grown up watching her mother's hands—scarred, rope-burned, strong as iron cable—work the harbor quarter of Verdant Strand. Minna the Rope-Merchant commanded the docks with a voice that could cut through storm-wind, and her daughter had inherited the timber of it but not yet the authority. Then the Remaking shattered the Dominion's tax-ships, and Minna sent her daughter out alone for the first time. "You take the Amber Runner to Crimport," Minna said, pressing a manifest into Jaren's hands. "Pre-Remaking rope in sealed barrels. The resistance networks are desperate for it—they're building new knots, new songs. Rope that won't sing the Dominion's ledger-spells."

"Mama, I've never navigated alone—"

"You've watched me do it since you could walk. And you've braided better knots than most sailors twice your age." Minna gripped her daughter's jaw, gentle but firm. "The Remaking didn't ask our permission either. Neither will I."

The voyage was seven days.

stories.title: The Drowned God's Emissary
stories.text: The Tide-Touched Scholar arrived in Greyport on 2026-08-06, dripping seawater that moved wrong—it flowed upward, defying gravity, carrying with it the smell of abyssal trenches and the song of dead god-things. Her name was lost. She'd been human once, five years ago, before she'd answered a summons in the Sapphire Deep and the Drowned God had answered back. Captain Merenna's three selves—Original, Echo, Mirror, all fractured by the Remaking into semi-autonomous versions of the same deepkin commander—had sent her as emissary. The message was simple and terrifying: the Tear of the Drowned God would fail within days unless one of two things happened. First: five willing souls from the surface-dweller kingdoms would descend to the boundary-waters and let the Drowned God drink their certainty, their sense of self. A blood-sacrifice, though the blood would be metaphysical—a slow, gentle dissolution into the god-thing's hunger. Second: the entire covenant would be renegotiated. No more mandatory sacrifice. Daily choice.

stories.title: The Glassblower's Sabotage
stories.text: Sella worked in the deepest kiln-house of Keshtir's Lampwick Quarter, where the furnace-songs made glass scream. The Dominion had conscripted her three years before the Remaking—a skilled hand, they said. Necessary. For the greater good of the State. For three years, she'd been forging weapon-glass. Consciousness-fragments melted into the molten glass, their awareness distributed through the material until the resulting blades could kill without hesitation, cut without mercy, obey without question. She was good at it. The auditors praised her. Advancement was promised. On 2026-08-06, Sella was working on a batch of glass-spears—fifty of them, each containing the dissolved consciousness of a refugee, each meant to arm a Dominion enforcer. She'd done this work a hundred times. But something had changed in the fragments. They weren't accepting dissolution anymore. They were fighting. Singing. She heard it as a high, keening frequency that made her teeth ache. The bone-singers had taught refusal-songs, and the fragments had learned. They didn't want to be weapons.

stories.title: The Starborn's First Question
stories.text: When Valorix hatched from the meteor-egg, the night sky broke. It wasn't sudden—more like a door opening in starlight. The griffin-creature unfurled wings of luminescence and ash, and where she moved through the air, the stars rearranged themselves into patterns nobody could read. In the High Moors, shepherds watched their flocks bolt in panic. In Ashwater village, children wept at the wrongness of it. Even the bone-singers paused their resistance-songs to listen. Ashara the Archer was in her hermitage when she felt it—a presence, ancient and bewildered, taking its first breath in a world that was broken. She found the creature at dawn, perched on a wind-scoured ridge where the old observatory had stood before the Remaking burned it. Valorix was impossibly large—larger than a horse, larger than reason—but she held herself as if uncertain of her own edges, as if her luminous wings might dissolve if she stopped concentrating. "What are you?" Ashara whispered.

stories.title: The Smuggler's Daughter
stories.text: Kessa had inherited her mother's cheekbones and her father's talent for reading tide-marks where they spelled safe passage through the Dominion's blockade. At twenty-three, she ran cargo out of Verdant Strand's harbor quarter—pre-Remaking silk, bioluminescent ink, consciousness-fragments destined for the Counter-Archive's waystation north of Pelimor. The work paid in silver and rumors. The Dominion auditors had begun stopping merchant vessels two weeks prior. They weren't searching for contraband; they were hunting refugees. Kessa had smuggled forty-seven people across the Sapphire Sea before the patrols tightened. Now, with her hull loaded and her crew nervous, she stood in the harbormaster's tower negotiating with Captain Vesta—ostensibly to bribe her way past the checkpoint, truly to learn if the rumors of a reef-passage were real. Vesta smiled with teeth filed to points. "You remind me of someone. A woman who stole my heart once, then stole a ship. We never did sort which theft was worse." She handed Kessa a chart marked in fading silver ink. "There's a route through the Rust Shoals. Corsairs use it.

stories.title: The Spice-Merchant's Threshold
stories.text: Raen stood at the Wailing Scar's edge where three markets bled into one another, watching the boundaries shimmer. The Remaking had made her a threshold-being—no longer fully surface, not yet deepkin, caught between worlds. Refugee caravans needed guides through the fractures, and the Dominion paid handsomely for intelligence on smuggler routes. She'd been running both sides for three seasons until a merchant asked her to choose. The spice-cargo she carried wasn't just cardamom—it was testimony. Refugees had woven their stories into the bundles, and Raen could feel them singing beneath her ribs. At the Wailing Scar's heart, she made her choice: neither Dominion nor Counter-Archive, but something new. A merchant of memory, not control.

stories.title: The Ironsmith's Reckoning
stories.text:
Morryn Ironfoot had forged blades for three kingdoms before the Remaking turned gold to ash. Now he forged blades for the Dominion auditors—weapons-glass that sang consciousness-fragments into compliance. The work paid in ration-stamps and the hollow knowledge that he was complicit in the machinery of extraction. When the auditor captain arrived at his forge in Keshtir's industrial quarter with a commission, Morryn's stomach dropped. The request was specific: a sword capable of severing any spoken truth, even oath-magic. It would take a master smith to craft. It would take blood-work. "I cannot," Morryn said flatly. "That blade—if it exists—would unmake covenant itself. It would break the Tear of the Drowned God. You're describing a weapon that would drown the surface world."

The auditor smiled. "Precisely. The Dominion seeks to renegotiate the boundary covenant. We require... leverage."

Morryn refused. For this, they took his daughter. They didn't harm her—not directly. They simply held her in the Quarantine-House deep beneath the administrative heart, alongside three hundred other hostages.

stories.title: The Deepkin Captain's Three Faces
stories.text: Kalith the Deepkin Captain existed as three versions of herself—Original, Echo, and Mirror—fragmented during the Remaking and unable to fully coalesce. Each held a different opinion on how to renew the boundary covenant. Each was right. Each was drowning the others in argument. Original Kalith advocated for the traditional: five willing sacrifices, blood on the pearl-beds, the Tear's renewal sealed for another thousand years. She was ancient and conservative, her scales worn pale from three centuries of faithful guardianship. Echo Kalith proposed radical reform: daily choice-covenants instead of singular sacrifice. Surface-dwellers would choose anew each day whether to hold the boundary. It would be exhausting, contingent, revolutionary. Mirror Kalith believed the boundary should shatter. Let the abyss rise and drown the surface kingdoms. Let the deepkin reclaim their full realm without compromise. The Council of Depths listened to all three and fractured into deadlock. The Tear weakened by the day. Within a week, the boundary would fail either way. On the final council session, a human emissary arrived—Merris, half-deepkin, half-surface, fluent in both geometries.

stories.title: The Cartographer's Mercy
stories.text: Henryk the blind cartographer had burned his eyes to prevent drawing the ninth map. The Counter-Archive had sent him south to Pale Crossing—the waystation where refugees from the Burned Expanse gathered before scattering toward sanctuary—to teach false cartography to apprentices. To teach them that maps could lie, that prophecy could be resisted, that the completion of the ninth iteration was not inevitable. He arrived to find the waystation in crisis. A child had arrived carrying a prophecy-ledger—one of the phantom-documents that the Dominion used to enforce inevitability. The ledger sang. It rewrote itself in real-time. And it had only one blank page left before completion. The child was perhaps eight years old. The refugees wanted to destroy her—or the ledger she carried. They feared what would happen when that final page filled. Henryk asked to hold the ledger. Blind, he felt only the vibration of the pages, the hum of the magic that kept rewriting reality into predetermined patterns. He understood then: prophecy was not truth.
